frame: The Murkle floated past a radio telescope. Someone had left this story beside it.
text: I was twelve when Mum let me sit in the visitors' gallery at Mission Control for the final hour of the Selene 4 mission. Below me, rows of engineers hunched over glowing screens, and the giant display at the front showed the capsule as a small white dot creeping around the curve of the Moon. At 8.14 pm, the dot slipped behind the Moon and the radio crackled into silence. Everyone knew this would happen: for forty-eight minutes, the Moon itself would block every signal. Nobody spoke. The only sound was the hum of the air conditioning. One engineer chewed his pen until it cracked. The flight director, a tall woman named Dr Ferris, stood perfectly still with her arms folded and her eyes fixed on the clock. At 9.02 pm, the dot reappeared, and a voice burst through the speakers, half laughing: 'Control, Selene 4. We're coming home, and we've brought you a rock shaped like a potato.' The room exploded into cheers. Mum hugged me so hard that my badge fell off. Dr Ferris told the gallery that the crew were safe and would splash down in three days. To this day, though, the astronauts have never said what they were laughing about when the radio came back on.

frame: The Murkle hitched a ride on a whale-watching boat. It found this log in a bunk.
text: Whale-watching log, Saturday. We left the harbour at seven, and by nine the skipper, Dee, had spotted a humpback mother and her calf about two hundred metres off the bow. I watched them through the binoculars for nearly an hour: the mother rolling lazily on the surface, the calf slapping its tail again and again as if it were practising. My cousin Rafi had gone out on the smaller research boat that morning, and over the radio he told us that his team had dropped an underwater microphone and recorded the mother singing. I would have given anything to hear it, but the radio was too crackly to play it back. Just before lunch, the pair dived and didn't come up again. Dee told us humpbacks can stay under for up to forty-five minutes, so we waited, eating soggy sandwiches and staring at the empty sea. A seagull stole half of mine. They never came back up where we could see them. We headed back to the harbour at three, sunburnt and quiet. Rafi says the recording is too precious to email, so I won't hear it until he gets home next month. Tonight, in my bunk, I keep wondering where the calf is now.

text: When we went away for the long weekend, Dad left our robot vacuum, Dusty, switched on to 'patrol mode', which he said would keep the house clean while we were gone. On Saturday, Dad and I checked the app on his phone. The little map showed Dusty's path as a neat blue line zigzagging around the lounge room. On Sunday morning, the blue line went through the dog flap, across the back lawn and under the side fence. Dad and I watched the live camera on Dusty's lid as it showed grass, then a garden gnome, then the inside of Mrs Agosti's chook shed. Dad went very quiet. Then he laughed so hard that he had to sit down on the sand. We were three hours away at the beach, so nobody could go and get it. We tried calling Mrs Agosti, but she was away too. When we finally got home on Monday night, Dusty was sitting in our driveway, fully charged, with a feather stuck to its brush and an egg balanced on its lid. Our dog sniffed it suspiciously. The camera had switched off at lunchtime on Sunday, so to this day nobody knows how it got home, or where the egg came from.

text: Lena had been practising her trumpet solo for six months, and the audition for the State Youth Band was at ten o'clock. Only performers were allowed in the room, so I waited in the corridor outside, pacing up and down the squeaky lino and trying not to bite my nails. Every few minutes, I checked my watch. Through the heavy wooden door, I heard her start. The first few notes wobbled, then steadied, and then the solo soared, so loud and bright that the cleaner down the hall stopped mopping to listen. Then it stopped, halfway through a phrase. There was a long silence. I pressed my ear against the door, but all I could make out was a murmur of low voices, as if the three judges were whispering to each other. Ten minutes later, Lena came out holding her trumpet case in both arms. Her face gave nothing away. Even her ears, which go red when she's upset, were their normal colour. 'Well?' I said. She shrugged and said they'd send a letter. In the car on the way home, she stared out of the window and hummed the solo over and over, but every time I asked what the judges had whispered, she turned up the radio.
